newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK to face pressure from China on taxes -- economist.
newsitem.headline: HK to face pressure from China on taxes -- economist.

text.p: Hong Kong was likely to face pressure to bring its tax system more in line with that of China in the medium to long term, Ian Perkin, chief economist and assistant director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, said on Wednesday.

"If you have a huge country like China and one little piece of it has special tax incentives, or a special tax system like Hong Kong does which offers incentives indirectly...all the development occurs there," Perkin told reporters at a business lunch.
"It is the sort of thing that the Chinese leadership in economics like (vice premier) Zhu Rongji have been very wary of," he said.

Perkin stressed this was not an immediate concern and would probably not show up within five years after Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese sovereignty at midnight June 30 this year, but added the pressure would be strong when it comes.
"I think it's going to take all the defensive powers of the new (Hong Kong) government" to resist, he said.

Hong Kong has been promised independence on economic and tax policies for 50 years after the handover. Taxes collected in Hong Kong may not be transferred to China, and Beijing may not levy taxes in the territory.

Hong Kong prides itself on its policy of low and simple taxes, and a survey by Coopers & Lybrand showed that companies agreed, with 84 percent of respondents voting Hong Kong's tax system as the best in the region.

But Perkin said Hong Kong's and China's tax systems were so different, and the territory was such an attractive place for Chinese firms to do business, that there would inevitably be pressures to bring the two systems closer.
He compared Hong Kong's position with that of China's special economic zones (SEZs), which boomed from their right to offer incentives aimed at attracting foreign investors.
Beijing is planning to gradually phase out SEZs' investment and tax privileges and equalise tax policies between them and other cities, in part to let backward inland areas catch up.
Perkin also noted the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar was safe while China's yuan was not fully convertible.
Once the yuan became fully convertible, which was probably five to 10 years out, then the Hong Kong dollar may be pegged to it or to a basket of currencies, he said.
